passage:
Age nine: On Monday, Disha heard from a classmate named Kamini that the old banyan by the gate was haunted. On Tuesday two more classmates said the same and added that a ghost had been seen at night. By Thursday Disha, who had never noticed anything odd near it, walked the long way round to the bus and told her little cousin that the tree was haunted, too. Each retelling made it feel more true.

Age twenty: Divyansh's phone lit up with a message warning that a common food was dangerous, forwarded from four different groups. It ended, 'Share with everyone you care about.' He had seen it so often that it felt like news, so he forwarded it to his hostel group. Bidisha replied, 'Where's the source? Did anyone check?' Some members sent thumbs-down. Divyansh felt a flash of irritation; Bidisha seemed cold about people's safety. Later he searched for the source. It came from a chain of copies with no name on it. He wrote to the group, 'I shouldn't have sent that before checking. Sorry.'

qa.q: What did the warning message end with?
How did repetition make an idea feel true for Disha and for Divyansh?
qa.a: Disha heard the haunted tree story from more classmates each day and believed it more after each retelling. Divyansh saw the message from four groups and took how often he saw it as proof, so he forwarded it before checking.

qa.q: What was Divyansh feeling when Bidisha asked for the source?
qa.a: A flash of irritation, because doubting the message seemed cold about people's safety, before he began to doubt it himself.

qa.q: What could Divyansh do before forwarding the next message?
qa.a: Look for the original source, and pause when many copies carry no name.

grounding: An idea made to feel true by repetition at nine and at twenty, in playground retellings and a forwarded scare message.
